difficultyReason: Three-step conditional chain with modus ponens at the end: A→B, B→C, A, therefore C. Traps (B) and (D) share topic or conclusion type but drop a link or reverse a conditional; trap (E) runs a two-premise chain rather than three.
stimulus: If the municipal bond measure passes, the library's endowment will grow. If the library's endowment grows, it will be able to hire a second archivist. The bond measure will pass. So the library will be able to hire a second archivist.
questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If the ice on the lake thickens, ice fishing will be permitted. If ice fishing is permitted, the bait shop will reopen. The ice on the lake will thicken. Therefore, the bait shop will reopen.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If the tax levy passes, the school will receive new computers. The tax levy will pass. So students will learn to code more quickly.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a candidate wins the primary, she will appear on the general-election ballot. Senator Park did not win the primary. Therefore, she will not appear on the general-election ballot.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If the rezoning vote succeeds, a new park will be built. If a new park is built, nearby property values will rise. Property values near the proposed park have already risen. Therefore, the rezoning vote will succeed.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If the referendum passes, the museum will expand. The referendum will pass. Therefore, the museum will expand.

explanations.correct: Stimulus is a three-step chain: A→B, B→C, A, ∴ C. (A) matches exactly: thickens→ice fishing, ice fishing→bait shop, thickens, ∴ bait shop reopens. Same conditional directions, same number of premises, same modus-ponens conclusion.
explanations.B: Matches topic (civic vote) and affirms the antecedent, but the conclusion ("students will learn to code more quickly") is an unlicensed new claim — the chain structure is broken.
explanations.C: Denies the antecedent — a two-premise modus tollens-lookalike, not a three-step affirming chain. Conclusion is negative, not positive.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent of the second conditional to reach the antecedent of the first — reverses the chain's direction. Not the same form.
explanations.E: Single conditional + modus ponens (two premises, not three). Drops the middle link.

difficultyReason: Universal generalization plus particular instantiation plus conditional: "All A are B; all B require C; x is A; therefore x requires C." Mixed forms force students to track both a syllogism and a conditional step.
stimulus: All amphibians are ectothermic. Every ectothermic vertebrate requires an external heat source to regulate its body temperature. The hellbender is an amphibian. Therefore, the hellbender requires an external heat source to regulate its body temperature.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All corporate bonds are debt instruments. Every debt instrument carries some default risk. The Marcor bond is a corporate bond. Therefore, the Marcor bond carries some default risk.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most songbirds migrate. Every migratory bird requires fat reserves before departure. The scarlet tanager is a songbird. Therefore, the scarlet tanager requires fat reserves before departure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: All mollusks have soft bodies. The nautilus has a soft body. Therefore, the nautilus is a mollusk.

choices.label: D
choices.text: All granite is igneous. The quarry stone is igneous. Every igneous rock resists weathering. Therefore, the quarry stone resists weathering.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most sonnets have fourteen lines. Every fourteen-line poem contains a volta. "Ozymandias" is a sonnet. Therefore, "Ozymandias" probably contains a volta.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: all A are B; all B require C; x is A; ∴ x requires C — two universal premises, one particular instance, universal (non-hedged) conclusion. (A) mirrors each step: all corporate bonds are debt instruments; all debt instruments carry default risk; Marcor is a corporate bond; therefore Marcor carries default risk.
explanations.B: Opens with "most" instead of "all," weakening the first premise's quantifier and breaking the universal-to-particular chain.
explanations.C: Affirms the consequent — having a soft body doesn't make something a mollusk. This is a two-premise flawed argument; the stimulus is valid.
explanations.D: Same premises present but in a different order that converts the middle step (quarry is igneous is asserted directly, not derived), and omits the universal "all granite is igneous" chain properly; closer structurally than B/C/E but mismatches premise order and derivation path.
explanations.E: Hedges with "most" and "probably" — conclusion strength is weakened, so it does not match the stimulus's universal conclusion.

difficultyReason: Disjunctive syllogism plus conditional: "A or B; A→C; ¬C; ∴ B." Students must recognize that the middle step is a contrapositive application that eliminates one disjunct.
stimulus: Either the manuscript was written by Beaumont or it was written by Fletcher. If Beaumont wrote the manuscript, the paper would bear a Kentish watermark. The paper does not bear a Kentish watermark. Therefore, Fletcher wrote the manuscript.
questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Either the diamond came from the Karowe mine or it came from the Letseng mine. If the diamond came from the Karowe mine, it would contain nitrogen inclusions. The diamond does not contain nitrogen inclusions. Therefore, the diamond came from the Letseng mine.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sample is either basalt or granite. It is basalt. Therefore, it is not granite.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If the package was shipped from Osaka, it would bear a customs stamp. The package bears a customs stamp. Therefore, the package was shipped from Osaka.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Either the violin was made by Guarneri or by Stradivari. If Guarneri made it, the f-holes would be asymmetrical. The f-holes are asymmetrical. Therefore, Guarneri made it.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Either the essay was written in 1640 or in 1650. If it was written in 1640, it would reference the regicide. The essay references the regicide. Therefore, the essay was written in 1640.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A∨B; A→C; ¬C; ∴ B. The middle step uses contrapositive (¬C→¬A) to eliminate a disjunct. (A) matches: Karowe∨Letseng; Karowe→nitrogen; ¬nitrogen; ∴ Letseng. Same disjunctive base, same contrapositive move, same positive conclusion about the surviving disjunct.
explanations.B: A bare disjunctive syllogism with no conditional middle step — two premises, not three.
explanations.C: Affirms the consequent — a classic fallacy; stimulus is valid, so this cannot be parallel.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent inside the conditional step — concludes the antecedent from the consequent, reversing the contrapositive move.
explanations.E: Same affirming-the-consequent move as D — invalid, and the stimulus is valid.

difficultyReason: Analogy-plus-universal: two shared properties justify inferring a third. Conclusion strength is hedged ("likely"). Students must match both the analogical form and the modal hedge.
stimulus: The economies of Varland and Neufeld share two key features: both are small open economies heavily dependent on commodity exports, and both peg their currencies to the euro. When commodity prices fell last decade, Varland experienced a sharp contraction. Neufeld is now facing a similar commodity price decline, so Neufeld will likely experience a sharp contraction as well.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The novels of Marin and Quilter share two key features: both employ unreliable first-person narrators, and both are set during wartime. Marin's novels have been widely translated. Quilter's novels share these features, so Quilter's novels will likely be widely translated as well.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cities of Portmouth and Callenby share two key features: both are coastal harbor towns, and both rely on fishing as their primary industry. When a red tide struck Portmouth last year, its fishing yields collapsed. Callenby is now experiencing a red tide, so Callenby's fishing yields will likely collapse as well.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cities of Portmouth and Callenby are both coastal harbor towns. When a red tide struck Portmouth, its fishing yields collapsed. Therefore, Callenby's fishing yields will collapse if a red tide strikes it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Several coastal cities have collapsed when hit by red tides. Callenby is a coastal city. Therefore, Callenby's fishing yields must collapse.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The cities of Portmouth and Callenby share many features. Portmouth's fishing yields collapsed last year. Therefore, Callenby's fishing yields collapsed last year too.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: X and Y share properties P and Q; when condition C struck X, X suffered outcome O; C is now striking Y; ∴ Y will likely suffer O. (B) mirrors each element: Portmouth/Callenby share two features; red tide caused a collapse in Portmouth; red tide now in Callenby; ∴ Callenby will likely collapse. Hedged conclusion preserved.
explanations.A: Matches surface structure of "two shared features," but the outcome being transferred (widely translated) is not triggered by a condition currently recurring in the second case — there is no parallel to the recurring commodity price decline / red tide.
explanations.C: Only one shared feature named; conclusion is a conditional, not a prediction. Missing the second shared property and the present-tense recurrence.
explanations.D: Draws from a general population ("several coastal cities") rather than a pairwise analogy; conclusion uses "must" instead of "likely," mismatching modal force.
explanations.E: Vague premise ("share many features") and past-tense conclusion — stimulus concludes about a future event.

difficultyReason: Contrapositive chain with three steps: A→B, B→C, ¬C, ∴ ¬A. Students must trace two contrapositive moves and match both the negative conclusion and the three-premise count.
stimulus: If a painting is genuinely by Vermeer, it contains ultramarine pigment in the shadow layers. If a painting contains ultramarine pigment in the shadow layers, X-ray fluorescence analysis will detect traces of lapis lazuli. X-ray fluorescence analysis of the disputed painting did not detect traces of lapis lazuli. Therefore, the disputed painting is not genuinely by Vermeer.
questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a fossil is from the Cambrian period, it predates the emergence of vertebrates. If a fossil predates the emergence of vertebrates, it will contain no hollow bone fragments. The specimen from Well Ridge contains no hollow bone fragments. Therefore, the specimen is from the Cambrian period.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a wine is a genuine Chablis, it comes from the Kimmeridgian limestone soils. If a wine comes from the Kimmeridgian limestone soils, it will exhibit a distinctive mineral note. The wine under review does not exhibit a distinctive mineral note. Therefore, the wine under review is not a genuine Chablis.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a building is a true Gothic cathedral, it has pointed arches. The building across the square does not have pointed arches. Therefore, it is not a true Gothic cathedral.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a coin is a genuine Roman denarius, it contains a high silver content. The coin in question contains a high silver content. Therefore, it is a genuine Roman denarius.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If a recording is from the 1950s, it is on magnetic tape. If a recording is on magnetic tape, it can be digitized with standard equipment. The studio recording from 1952 can be digitized with standard equipment. Therefore, the studio recording is from the 1950s.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A→B, B→C, ¬C, ∴ ¬A — three premises, chained contrapositive ending in negation of original antecedent. (B) mirrors it precisely: Chablis→Kimmeridgian, Kimmeridgian→mineral note, ¬mineral note, ∴ not Chablis.
explanations.A: Affirms the final consequent (no hollow bones) and concludes the original antecedent — that's affirming the consequent, which is invalid. The stimulus is valid.
explanations.C: Two-premise modus tollens, not a three-premise chain. Drops the middle conditional.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent in a two-premise argument — invalid.
explanations.E: Three conditionals but ends with affirming-the-consequent move to conclude the antecedent — invalid, and also the conclusion is positive, not negative.

difficultyReason: Universal generalization + conditional + modus ponens. Three-step mixed form requires matching the universal quantifier, conditional chain, and particular conclusion — not just one of these.
stimulus: Every language that distinguishes grammatical gender marks it on nouns. If a language marks gender on nouns, it also marks gender on adjectives that modify those nouns. Icelandic distinguishes grammatical gender. Therefore, Icelandic marks gender on adjectives that modify nouns.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every jurisdiction that recognizes community property divides marital assets equally at divorce. If a jurisdiction divides marital assets equally at divorce, it also applies the same rule to debts acquired during the marriage. The state of Tarmouth recognizes community property. Therefore, Tarmouth applies the equal-division rule to debts acquired during the marriage.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Most jurisdictions that recognize community property divide marital assets equally at divorce. If a jurisdiction divides marital assets equally, it also applies the same rule to debts. The state of Tarmouth recognizes community property. Therefore, Tarmouth probably applies the equal-division rule to debts.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every jurisdiction that recognizes community property divides marital assets equally. Tarmouth divides marital assets equally. Therefore, Tarmouth recognizes community property.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a jurisdiction recognizes community property, it divides marital assets equally. Tarmouth divides marital assets equally. Therefore, Tarmouth recognizes community property.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every jurisdiction that recognizes community property divides marital assets equally at divorce. Tarmouth recognizes community property. Therefore, Tarmouth divides marital assets equally at divorce.

explanations.correct: Stimulus structure: all A are B; B→C; x is A; ∴ x is C — universal premise feeds an instance into a conditional chain. (A) matches: all community-property jurisdictions do X; X→Y; Tarmouth is a community-property jurisdiction; ∴ Tarmouth does Y. Same three-step mixed form with universal conclusion.
explanations.B: Weakens the first premise's quantifier to "most" and hedges the conclusion with "probably" — strength shift.
explanations.C: Affirms the consequent — reverses the universal into a biconditional improperly. Invalid.
explanations.D: Same affirming-the-consequent error, now on a conditional premise. Invalid.
explanations.E: Correct universal-to-particular step but drops the middle conditional — only two premises where the stimulus has three.

difficultyReason: Disjunctive syllogism with a universal-instantiation middle step: "A or B; every A has property P; this x lacks P; ∴ x is B." Mixed disjunctive + universal forms across three premises.
stimulus: The archaeological layer at Site 9 dates from either the Early Bronze Age or the Middle Bronze Age. Every Early Bronze Age layer at this region's sites contains tin-rich bronze fragments. The layer at Site 9 contains no tin-rich bronze fragments. Therefore, the layer at Site 9 dates from the Middle Bronze Age.
questionStem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most parallel to that in the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The fabric swatch was produced in either the 18th or the 19th century. Every 18th-century swatch of this type contains handspun linen fibers. The fabric swatch contains no handspun linen fibers. Therefore, the fabric swatch was produced in the 19th century.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The fabric swatch was produced in either the 18th or the 19th century. Most 18th-century swatches of this type contain handspun linen fibers. The fabric swatch contains no handspun linen fibers. Therefore, the fabric swatch was probably produced in the 19th century.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The fabric swatch was produced in the 18th century. Every 18th-century swatch contains handspun linen fibers. Therefore, the fabric swatch contains handspun linen fibers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every 18th-century swatch contains handspun linen fibers. The fabric swatch contains handspun linen fibers. Therefore, the fabric swatch was produced in the 18th century.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The fabric swatch was produced in the 18th or 19th century. The fabric swatch contains no handspun linen fibers. Therefore, the fabric swatch was produced in the 19th century.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A∨B; all A have P; this x lacks P; ∴ x is B. Three premises, universal + disjunctive middle, positive conclusion about surviving disjunct. (A) matches each step: 18th∨19th; every 18th-century swatch has P; this swatch lacks P; ∴ 19th century.
explanations.B: "Most" weakens the universal premise and "probably" hedges the conclusion — strength mismatch on both quantifier and modal force.
explanations.C: Categorical syllogism, not a disjunction-elimination argument. Conclusion is about the property, not about which disjunct holds.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent — invalid; the stimulus is valid.
explanations.E: Drops the universal premise about 18th-century swatches entirely, so the contrapositive move that licenses the elimination is missing.

difficultyReason: Three-step conditional chain with modus tollens: A→B, B→C, ¬C, ∴ ¬A. Requires distinguishing from nearby modus ponens chains and from two-premise contrapositive shortcuts.
stimulus: If a server handles peak traffic without latency spikes, it must have sufficient cache capacity. If a server has sufficient cache capacity, its disk-access logs will show low read frequencies during peak hours. The disk-access logs for server Delta show high read frequencies during peak hours. Therefore, server Delta does not handle peak traffic without latency spikes.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: If a chef earns a Michelin star, she must source her produce locally. If a chef sources her produce locally, her supplier invoices will show regional farm names. Chef Okafor's supplier invoices show no regional farm names. Therefore, Chef Okafor has not earned a Michelin star.

choices.label: B
choices.text: If a chef earns a Michelin star, she must source her produce locally. If a chef sources her produce locally, her supplier invoices will show regional farm names. Chef Okafor's supplier invoices show regional farm names. Therefore, Chef Okafor has earned a Michelin star.

choices.label: C
choices.text: If a chef earns a Michelin star, her supplier invoices show regional farm names. Chef Okafor's supplier invoices show no regional farm names. Therefore, Chef Okafor has not earned a Michelin star.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most chefs who earn a Michelin star source their produce locally. If a chef sources her produce locally, her supplier invoices will show regional farm names. Chef Okafor's supplier invoices show no regional farm names. Therefore, Chef Okafor has probably not earned a Michelin star.

choices.label: E
choices.text: If a chef earns a Michelin star, she must source her produce locally. Chef Okafor sources her produce locally. Therefore, Chef Okafor has earned a Michelin star.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A→B, B→C, ¬C, ∴ ¬A — three premises, chained modus tollens. (A) mirrors each step: Michelin→local sourcing, local sourcing→regional invoices, ¬regional invoices, ∴ ¬Michelin.
explanations.B: Affirms the final consequent (invoices show farm names) and concludes the antecedent — invalid, and the stimulus is valid.
explanations.C: Two-premise modus tollens; drops the middle conditional. Premise count mismatch.
explanations.D: Weakens the first premise to "most" and hedges the conclusion with "probably" — strength shift on both the universal and the modal.
explanations.E: Two-premise affirming-the-consequent-style argument with a positive conclusion — invalid and oppositely directed.

difficultyReason: Mixed form: universal premise about a category, instantiation to a member, and a conditional step that licenses a positive conclusion. Students must match the universal strength and the number of inferential steps.
stimulus: Every virus in the Flaviviridae family replicates using an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase. If a pathogen replicates using an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase, it is susceptible to nucleoside analog antivirals. The dengue virus belongs to the Flaviviridae family. Therefore, the dengue virus is susceptible to nucleoside analog antivirals.
questionStem: The reasoning in the argument above is most similar to the reasoning in which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every statute enacted under the Commerce Clause regulates interstate activity. If a statute regulates interstate activity, it can preempt conflicting state laws. The Mercer Act was enacted under the Commerce Clause. Therefore, the Mercer Act can preempt conflicting state laws.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Many statutes enacted under the Commerce Clause regulate interstate activity. If a statute regulates interstate activity, it can preempt conflicting state laws. The Mercer Act was enacted under the Commerce Clause. Therefore, the Mercer Act probably can preempt conflicting state laws.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every statute enacted under the Commerce Clause regulates interstate activity. The Mercer Act regulates interstate activity. Therefore, the Mercer Act was enacted under the Commerce Clause.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a statute was enacted under the Commerce Clause, it can preempt conflicting state laws. The Mercer Act can preempt conflicting state laws. Therefore, the Mercer Act was enacted under the Commerce Clause.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every statute enacted under the Commerce Clause regulates interstate activity. The Mercer Act was enacted under the Commerce Clause. Therefore, the Mercer Act regulates interstate activity.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: all A do P; P→Q; x is A; ∴ x does Q. Three premises, universal + conditional, universal-strength conclusion. (A) matches: all Commerce Clause statutes regulate interstate activity; regulation→preemption; Mercer is a Commerce Clause statute; ∴ Mercer can preempt.
explanations.B: "Many" weakens the universal, and "probably" hedges the conclusion — strength shift on both premise and conclusion.
explanations.C: Affirms the consequent of the universal — invalid. Stimulus is valid.
explanations.D: Affirms the consequent of the conditional — invalid.
explanations.E: Valid but drops the middle conditional; two premises where the stimulus has three.

difficultyReason: Disjunction with contrapositive elimination producing a negative conclusion about the other disjunct's property: A∨B; A→C; x is ¬B; ∴ x is C. Tests whether students can apply the disjunctive elimination in the opposite direction.
stimulus: Every work in the exhibition is either a lithograph or an etching. If a work is a lithograph, it was printed from a flat stone surface. The work titled "Harbor at Dusk" is not an etching. Therefore, "Harbor at Dusk" was printed from a flat stone surface.
questionStem: Which one of the following arguments is most similar in its reasoning to the argument above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every sonata on the program is either a Classical sonata or a Romantic sonata. If a sonata is Classical, it follows strict sonata-allegro form. The "Hoffmann Sonata" is not a Romantic sonata. Therefore, the "Hoffmann Sonata" follows strict sonata-allegro form.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Every sonata on the program is either Classical or Romantic. Most Classical sonatas follow strict sonata-allegro form. The "Hoffmann Sonata" is not Romantic. Therefore, the "Hoffmann Sonata" probably follows strict sonata-allegro form.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every sonata on the program is either Classical or Romantic. If a sonata is Classical, it follows strict sonata-allegro form. The "Hoffmann Sonata" is Classical. Therefore, the "Hoffmann Sonata" follows strict sonata-allegro form.

choices.label: D
choices.text: If a sonata is Classical, it follows strict sonata-allegro form. The "Hoffmann Sonata" does not follow strict sonata-allegro form. Therefore, the "Hoffmann Sonata" is not Classical.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Every sonata on the program is either Classical or Romantic. If a sonata is Romantic, it does not follow strict sonata-allegro form. The "Hoffmann Sonata" follows strict sonata-allegro form. Therefore, the "Hoffmann Sonata" is Classical.

explanations.correct: Stimulus: A∨B; A→C; x is ¬B; ∴ x is C. The ¬B premise forces x into the A disjunct by elimination, and A→C delivers the positive conclusion. (A) matches exactly: Classical∨Romantic; Classical→strict form; ¬Romantic; ∴ strict form.
explanations.B: Quantifier weakened to "most," conclusion hedged with "probably" — strength shift on both.
explanations.C: Directly asserts the Classical disjunct rather than deriving it by eliminating the other — removes the disjunctive-elimination step. Only two relevant premises.
explanations.D: Pure two-premise modus tollens with no disjunctive premise — drops the disjunction entirely.
explanations.E: Different conditional (Romantic→¬strict) and reaches conclusion by affirming a property to pick the disjunct — the direction of reasoning is reversed.
